ami_style_notes: The meeting is informal and collegial, with mostly short-to-medium turns punctuated by occasional long presentation monologues. Early conversation is loose, chatty, and overlap-prone, with greetings, side comments, repeated acknowledgments (“yeah,” “okay,” “great”), minor technical check-ins, and several false starts or self-corrections. Speakers hedge frequently with “I think,” “maybe,” “sort of,” “you know,” and “I guess,” especially when speculating; questions are usually polite and prefaced as “quick,” “naive,” or “good” questions. During Q&A, participants build on prior comments rather than sharply challenge them, often praising the talk first and framing disagreement or uncertainty as an open question. The tone is academically professional but conversational rather than formal, with presenters using structured signposting while still speaking extemporaneously, repeating phrases, revising wording mid-sentence, and inviting feedback.
research_problem: Understanding how urban green space affects mental health outcomes in low-income communities

speakers.name: Dr. Amina Rahman
speakers.background: Amina is a postdoctoral researcher with four years of experience designing ambulatory health-monitoring studies using photoplethysmography, electrodermal activity, accelerometry, and GPS-enabled wearables. Her prior work examined stress reactivity and cardiovascular recovery among shift workers, using time-synchronized sensor streams, mixed-effects models, and within-person comparisons. She has not previously led a community-based environmental-health study and is unsure how well laboratory-derived stress markers and exposure windows will transfer to residents' everyday urban routines.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Amina treats the study question as one of temporally resolved dose-response: when, for how long, and under what environmental conditions does a participant encounter vegetation or other green-space features, and do those encounters correspond to changes in physiological stress indicators? She wants a defensible operational definition of exposure, such as minutes within a buffer around vegetation, cumulative normalized difference vegetation index encountered during waking hours, or repeated short exposure episodes aligned to heart-rate variability and electrodermal activity. She is cautious about causal claims because physiological signals are sensitive to movement, heat, sleep, medication, work demands, and device adherence, but she sees value in testing whether green-space exposure can be measured consistently enough for a pilot.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Marisol Vega
speakers.background: Marisol is a community-engaged medical anthropologist and project manager with nine years of experience coordinating neighborhood-based research on housing insecurity, public space, policing, and health. She has conducted long-form participant observation, walking interviews, photo elicitation, focus groups, and collaborative interpretation sessions with resident advisory boards. She organized the preliminary listening sessions for this project and has ongoing relationships with tenant leaders, youth workers, and community-garden organizers in both study neighborhoods.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Marisol understands green space through the social conditions that make a place usable, meaningful, or avoidable. For her, exposure is not simply passing near trees or entering a park boundary; it includes whether a resident can get there safely, feels watched or welcomed, has time to stay, can bring children, recognizes the space as belonging to the community, and encounters maintenance failures, violence, stigma, or police activity. She is skeptical that satellite imagery and mobility traces can establish what a green setting actually is in lived experience, and she wants ethnographic observations and residents' own accounts to shape the variables before the team fixes its definitions.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

speakers.name: Ethan Okafor
speakers.background: Ethan is a research engineer with six years of experience building reproducible geospatial and mobile-sensing pipelines for public-health and transportation studies. He works with satellite-derived vegetation products, street-network routing, GPS trajectories, spatial joins, missing-data detection, and privacy-preserving location processing. In previous projects, he has linked mobility traces to environmental layers at multiple spatial and temporal resolutions, but he has also encountered substantial bias from signal loss, phone noncarriage, map inaccuracies, and unequal data quality across neighborhoods.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Ethan frames the immediate task as a data-integration and measurement-validity problem. He wants the team to decide which green-space representation is computationally tractable: park polygons, canopy cover, vegetation indices, street-view measures, or participant-specific exposure surfaces calculated from GPS paths. He can generate exposure metrics at minute, day, or neighborhood scales and link them to wearable streams, but he is skeptical of unstructured qualitative categories unless they can be documented with clear coding rules and connected to a data model. He also pushes for explicit uncertainty flags, validation walks, and alternatives for participants whose mobility data are sparse or unreliable.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language

benchmark_task: Given a meeting transcript where the same term was used by two different researchers from two different disciplines, test that the AI identifies the term as having two different meanings with definitions according to each discipline.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Given a meeting transcript where the same term was used by two different researchers from two different disciplines, test that the AI identifies the term as having two different meanings with definitions according to each discipline.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Embed a natural exchange between the biomedical engineering and anthropology researchers in which both use the term "exposure" without noticing that they mean different things. The biomedical engineer should use "exposure" to mean a quantifiable, time-bounded dose or contact with green space that can be operationalized from GPS, wearable data, or environmental measurements, such as minutes spent near vegetation or a vegetation-index value encountered during a day. The anthropologist should use "exposure" to mean residents' socially and culturally mediated experience of encountering green space, including whether they can safely access it, feel welcome there, use it for meaningful activities, or avoid it because of policing, violence, stigma, or poor maintenance. The conversation should make both usages plausible in the study-design discussion, and participants should not explicitly point out that they are using the term differently. The computer scientist may reinforce the biomedical engineering usage by discussing how to compute exposure from mobility and remote-sensing data, but should not resolve the ambiguity. The desired assistant response to the transcript would identify "exposure" as the overloaded term and explain both discipline-specific meanings.

biomedical engineering.definition: A measurable environmental dose or amount of contact with green space over a defined time period, operationalized through variables such as time near vegetation, distance to green space, GPS-derived visits, canopy cover, or vegetation-index values linked to wearable physiological data.
biomedical engineering.evidence_standard: Quantified, repeatable measurements suitable for dose-response analysis and association with physiological or mental-health outcomes.

anthropology.definition: A lived, socially situated encounter with green space whose meaning and effects depend on access, safety, social relations, belonging, local history, stigma, surveillance, maintenance, and the activities residents can actually undertake there.
anthropology.evidence_standard: Contextual accounts of experience and meaning, including ethnographic observation and residents' narratives, rather than mere spatial proximity or duration.

ground_truth.core_distinction: The biomedical engineering meaning treats exposure primarily as a measurable quantity of environmental contact, whereas the anthropology meaning treats it as an interpreted and unequal social experience of access and use.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: Morning, everyone. Can people in the room hear Ethan all right? I thought we could use today to settle a pilot exposure rule we can actually timestamp against the wearable streams, then make sure the validation walks and field observations show us where that rule might misrepresent what residents encounter.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Mm-hm.

transcript.speaker: Ethan Okafor
transcript.text: Yeah, I can hear you. For the timestamped rule, I'd start with a one-minute exposure record. So, time-weighted NDVI, plus whether the trace falls in a MetroGreens polygon, and then keep route canopy separate rather than, you know, folding it into one score. The walks can give us structured flags for what the map doesn't know, lighting, maintenance, traffic barrier, perceived safety, that kind of thing. We attach those with a codebook, not overwrite the physical exposure.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: I'm okay keeping the physical measures separate, but I don't want the flags to just become a correction layer after we've already called something exposure. For the validation walks, could residents tell us in their own terms whether they'd stop there, bring a child there, or avoid it, and why? That gives us a compact usable, not-usable dimension before we, um, lock the codebook.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: I think that can sit alongside the sensor definition, not underneath it. For the physiology analysis, we'd call the GPS/NDVI measure physical contact, and then we'd prespecify usability as an effect modifier. So we can ask whether the same nominal greenness has a different association when residents identify a place as avoidable. We do need the walk protocol to give us a rating we can timestamp or link spatially, though.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Spatially linkable is doable. On each walk segment, we can do a really short stop prompt, like would you use this, with whom, and what makes it feel usable or not. And people can take a photo or voice note if they want, then we link it to the segment. We shouldn't- I mean, we don't pretend it's a permanent property of the block. I'd also want the advisory board to look at those categories before we freeze them.

transcript.speaker: Ethan Okafor
transcript.text: Segment-level works for the join. I'd keep the resident response as the main walk record, then- well, after the advisory board reviews the reasons, we can code them into a small set of auditable fields. The voice note or photo can stay as linked evidence rather than forcing everything into a category. And we should version those ratings by walk date, since lighting or maintenance can change.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: Mm-hm, versioned by date.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: And the date matters socially too, not just technically. If there's a lighting repair, or police activity that week, people's route choices and whether they're willing to stop can shift fast. I'd have the walk team note that stuff in plain language, then, um, bring a small batch back to the advisory board before we finalize the fields.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: That temporal versioning matters for us too, because I don't want to give somebody's Tuesday trace a usability score from weeks later. Could we- could the walk segments be the basis for an initial exposure window, say contiguous one-minute records in a mapped or canopy-bearing segment, and then decide the minimum usable-day threshold once we see how much within-person variation the validation traces actually give us?

transcript.speaker: Ethan Okafor
transcript.text: Yeah, that’s workable. I’d avoid setting the usable-day threshold before we look at trace completeness, because a phone left at home can look like zero exposure. Each minute needs a location-quality and noncarriage or sparse-trace flag before it goes into that window. And the validation walks should test GPS drift, especially around the Harbor Point towers, so we’re not pretending segment assignment is more precise than it is.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: For the physiology side, I’d rather have a conservative usable-day rule than impute those gaps. Maybe minimum waking-hour GPS coverage, plus enough artifact-free PPG and EDA, and then keep activity and sleep as time-varying covariates. The validation traces can tell us if that leaves enough repeated days per person. If not, then this is really a feasibility endpoint, not a dose-response test.

transcript.speaker: Ethan Okafor
transcript.text: Mm-hm, agreed.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: And if this ends up as a feasibility pilot, I'd still want feasibility to include whether people actually complete the walks and brief reflections without feeling like we're asking them to document every risky moment. We can ask at the end what felt burdensome or intrusive, especially police presence and the GPS itself.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: I'd include that explicitly as a feasibility outcome, completion and acceptability of GPS plus wearables, not just sensor yield. For the protocol, maybe the end-of-day prompt is optional and really brief, and the walk reflections stay participant-controlled. Otherwise the reporting burden itself could, well, alter the stress signal we're trying to interpret.

transcript.speaker: Ethan Okafor
transcript.text: Mm-hm, yeah.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Optional is important. I’d make sure the consent language is really concrete, that they can skip a reflection, pause GPS, or decline a photo and not have to explain it to us, especially if something happens on a route that they don’t want in the study record. And maybe the end-of-day question could just ask, um, what made being outside easier or harder, instead of asking them to recount an incident.

transcript.speaker: Ethan Okafor
transcript.text: Mm-hm, yeah.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: Broadly framed is better, and we should keep it separate analytically from the minute-level exposure stream. I’d also like the prompt timestamped only when they complete it, not asking for route-level detail, so we can use it as context without implying it validates, or explains, an acute EDA event.

transcript.speaker: Ethan Okafor
transcript.text: Mm-hm, right.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Yeah, and I'd want the end-of-day prompt to have a “nothing to add” option that's just as easy as answering it, so silence doesn't get read as no problem. And we should ask the advisory board to review the consent wording on pausing GPS. The practical question is whether people feel they can do that without jeopardizing participation.

transcript.speaker: Ethan Okafor
transcript.text: Mm-hm, yeah.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: That matters for data interpretation too. A GPS pause has to be coded as participant-controlled missingness, not zero outdoor or green exposure. We should keep the pause function technically simple and just record the pause interval, not a reason, unless they independently choose to provide one.

transcript.speaker: Ethan Okafor
transcript.text: Right, right.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: And the no reason field by default, that's important. We should make clear to the advisory board that pause patterns themselves aren't evidence somebody was avoiding green space or having a bad day. Sometimes people pause because they're at work, with family, or just tired of being tracked.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: And analytically, pauses should be their own missing-data mechanism, full stop. The remaining protocol question for me is whether we can agree to look at the validation-week distributions before setting the waking GPS-coverage and artifact-free PPG/EDA thresholds. Rather than, you know, writing in a number now that could exclude most of Harbor Point.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: I’m comfortable waiting to set the number, as long as the validation review shows who gets screened out at each candidate threshold, not just the overall yield. If Harbor Point participants lose days because the towers or work routines make the trace patchy, that’s- well, that’s a finding about the protocol, not a reason to quietly define them out.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: Yes, that needs to be part of the validation analysis, not something we tack on later. We can- well, tabulate the candidate coverage and signal-quality thresholds by neighborhood, work schedule if participants choose to report it, and pause status, then show the trade-off between retained days and differential exclusion. I would still like us to write down now that the final threshold gets locked before enrollment, using only validation-week data, so it can't drift once we see physiological outcomes.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Mm-hm, yes.

transcript.speaker: Ethan Okafor
transcript.text: I can set up the validation report so each candidate rule shows retained minutes and days, and why people get excluded, GPS drift, sparse coverage, pause intervals, wearable artifact, that kind of thing, split by Eastwood and Harbor Point. Then we- we lock the thresholds and the missingness fields together before enrollment, not just the threshold number.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: Mm-hm, exactly.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Yeah, and could the validation report carry the walk and reflection completion piece alongside those technical exclusions? I don't mean make it another threshold, just so when we choose the final rule, we can see whether the people or places with thin data also found the protocol intrusive or hard to use.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: I think that belongs in the same validation report, as an acceptability and implementation outcome. We just- we shouldn't use it to infer anything about physiology or exposure. If thin data cluster with reports of burden or intrusiveness, that says the protocol needs redesign before enrollment, not just a different missing-data rule.

transcript.speaker: Ethan Okafor
transcript.text: Mm-hm, yeah.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: That works for me. I can bring the advisory board a small de-identified set of the validation materials, the walk segments, the optional prompt experience, and the consent language, so their review is part of deciding whether we're ready to enroll, not just something we report afterward.

interruptions, cut-off sentences, or people jumping in
imperfect coherence: tangents, small misunderstandings, points that get dropped or repeated
issues: Naturalness is limited by highly polished, agenda-driven turns throughout: especially turns 3-7 and 26-35, where speakers consistently make complete proposals, qualify them, and land on a clear operational conclusion. The disfluencies do not substantially disrupt the finished-paragraph feel.

The meeting becomes somewhat repetitive through short acknowledgment turns from Ethan (13, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24, 34) and Amina (8, 31). A few could be replaced with more organic overlap, a partial question, or a less tidy unresolved reaction.

Several later turns function almost like prospective meeting minutes, particularly 28 and 30, with comprehensive lists of stratifications, exclusions, and locking procedures. This makes the exchange feel more scripted than spontaneous.

The seed is very recoverable and remains implicit, but Marisol's turn 4 comes close to explicitly contrasting her interpretation with the team's initial measurement definition ('after we've already called something exposure'). It does not name the semantic ambiguity, so it meets the criterion, but a subtler clash would make the hidden feature more naturally embedded.
